title: The Geonim
hookLine: heads of the Babylonian academies answer questions from Jews across the world

cards: A community in Kairouan, in North Africa, has a question it can't settle. Not about a holiday or a meal. A history question: how was the Mishnah written?

And the Talmud, how did it come together? Who did what, and in what order? So Rabbi Jacob ben Nissim, a teacher there, writes a letter and sends it a very long way east, to the head of the academy at Pumbedita.
And an answer comes back: long, careful, and so useful that people are still reading it.

teach.b: After the Talmud was sealed, the academies of Sura and Pumbedita went on, and their heads came to carry a title: Gaon, in the plural Geonim.
It's usually explained as short for the head of the academy that is the pride of Jacob, a phrase from a psalm, which in the 1917 Jewish translation reads "The pride of Jacob whom He loveth."
In everyday Hebrew, gaon came to mean a genius. But here it's a job title, and the job was to teach, and to answer. Jewish communities were spread across a huge distance.

The Talmud was their shared text, but it is long and hard, and real life keeps producing cases it never quite covered. So letters traveled to the Geonim, who read the question, studied it, and wrote back.

teach.h: THE LETTER OF RAV SHERIRA GAON.
teach.b: The letter from Kairouan reached Rav Sherira Gaon, head of Pumbedita. His reply, known as the Letter of Rav Sherira Gaon, walks through how the Mishnah and the Talmud took shape, teacher by teacher.
Here's the picture: letters across the world.

A text sealed in one place, and a web of letters spreading it to many others; a question written in one city, an answer in another, and the conversation of the academies reaching people who had never seen them.

how: Jews today still turn to the Geonim's surviving letters and rulings as early witnesses to how the Talmud was read, and historians study the Letter of Rav Sherira Gaon for its account of the Mishnah and Talmud.

games.q: you're a teacher in Kairouan. your community can't settle how the Mishnah and Talmud came to be written. what do you do?
o: make your best guess and teach it.
write a letter to the head of the academy at Pumbedita.
drop the question; it doesn't matter.
games.why: they wrote east, and Rav Sherira Gaon's long reply walks through how the Mishnah and Talmud took shape, teacher by teacher.

practice: Let a real question come to mind, not a quiz question but one you actually carry, about your tradition, your family's story, a text you never understood.

Don't answer it; just find the words for it, clear enough that someone far away could understand, the way the people of Kairouan found theirs. If you pray, you can bring that question to God as it is.
